translations.text: Once, when those honored before us [?] the grace of God and sounded their devout melodies, all of us were there with you. United in the word of truth, we learned the same things, rejoiced in the same things, and delighted in them. No one among those who understand what is good takes any pleasure for himself, but does everything for the glory of God. Whoever agrees with the speaker shares in the giver’s gift, for by praising the speaker he worships the one being proclaimed. Our fathers taught us this conduct free from envy, especially our father, who is the head of all the fathers and sits on the honored throne above them all, whose mind is clear and holy, free from jealousy. He himself first composes the skillful spiritual song and makes it sound melodiously in everyone’s ears: “Who would make all the people of God prophets?” Such is the spirit that glorifies its Lord and regards the words and good qualities of others as its own. If anyone disparages the words of others, he turns not against the one who received the grace, but against the one who gave it. Thoughts are revealed in the face. Look at the father of us all: see how he looks with a cheerful face and kindly eyes upon us who speak and upon you who listen. When you see someone’s face cast down, take note of the deceit in his thoughts. When his face hangs down, know that his heart is plotting deceit, as Scripture also says: “Whoever winks with his eye plots deceit.”

Christ is glorified, and the world is enlightened. But the one who harbors evil in his mind sits with his heart torn, his liver rent, and a deep wound within him. Since we have found a father who is holy and free from envy, we have learned without deceit, and we will impart what we have learned without envy. Let us begin the sequence that we were following yesterday and left unfinished because of the abundance of various thoughts pouring in from here and there. We had the intention of explaining a little of the beginning of the Gospel. I do not know how the dispute [?] with the heretics that arose in our midst diverted us—not by passing from one subject to another, but by attending to that same subject and those same thoughts. Christ is glorified, and the battle against those who fight Christ is set in order. Let every evil passion be rejected. Let those who today celebrate the festival of stumbling and delusion be ashamed: it is a mere name, devoid of the truth of proper observance.

Those who have put on Christ celebrate Passover with the Jews. Those clothed in Christ share fellowship with those who fight Christ. I call them clothed in Christ because of the name they profess. But what fellowship can there be between light and darkness? What agreement is there between the Jews and Christ? What correspondence is there between Christ’s table and the Jews’ [?] table? The children of godliness celebrate Passover with dogs. Those who ought to sing praises with the angels howl with dogs. The godly person praises with the angels: “I will give thanks to you, Lord, with my whole heart; before your angels I will sing psalms to you.” The godly person gives glory with the angels, but whoever overturns the order of the Church howls out the festival with dogs. And to show that these are not words of insult, but of truth and rebuke, listen to Paul, the great preacher, who says: “Beware of the dogs; beware of the evil workers.”

Let us see where the Jews stand and what condition the Christians are in. Listen to the holy Gospel: “Whoever believes in the Son,” it says, “receives eternal life; and whoever disobeys the Son does not see life.” The living celebrate a feast with the dead. What good have the Jews devised? What order of worship have they preserved uncorrupted, so that you might draw from them beautiful practices to add as a necessary support to the Church? Do you not hear the prophet saying, “You, house of Israel, have acted perversely throughout your youth and falsified the truth”? For they denied the worship of God and sold it, because they paid no heed. Indeed, they did not even keep their wine pure. Is this not the very first accusation against them in the prophet Isaiah? “Your merchants,” he says, “mix water with wine.” If only the heretics now mixed water with wine, and not God with created beings! See the prophets’ written accusation against the Jews, which the apostles also proclaim openly. Listen to the great preacher Paul, who writes to the Thessalonians: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that you too have suffered the same things from your own people as the Church of God has from the Jews—from the Jews who killed the Lord Jesus and their own prophets and persecuted us, who also displeased God and opposed mankind.” Do you become a partner of those who are subject to immeasurable punishments? To such people Isaiah says, “That is your portion, and that is the lot of your inheritance.”

I would like to learn from them why they celebrate the feast at all, and for the sake of what hope, since they do away with repentance. What worship do they practice—vain and [?], the worship of the foolish? They do it without hope of repentance, though they need repentance more than anyone. Burning with sores, they deny the physician. They go about bearing the name of Cathars, which means “the holy ones,” yet they have holiness neither in body nor in mind. Nothing so provokes God, brings him to anger, and makes someone liable to severe torments as calling oneself holy. Even if someone is free from every sin, he ought to count himself among sinners. Listen to Saint John: “Children, if we sin, we are not of God”; and again, “Whoever does evil is not of God.” After giving instruction not to sin, he then brings forward the truth. The one who said, “Whoever sins is not of God,” lowers himself still further and says this also: “If we say that we have not sinned, we lie.” He gave instruction in watchfulness, and did not deny the power. He looked to the teaching of truth, and also saw how readily the mind stumbles. But now the enemies of honoring God celebrate feasts and demand confirmation for their deeds, while they have strayed from every firm foundation.

I too wished to raise such matters with you who love Christ, and to show that this opposition is futile, an empty opinion. When someone departs from the order of the Church, he does not stand still; rather, error carries him away, like the currents of rivers flowing into the sea. What do Easter and the feast make known? What is accomplished on the day of the feast? Are not Christ’s sufferings and resurrection [?] proclaimed? Salvation is announced to the world, and every soul is enlightened by the divine word. How, then, do we possess this seal and pledge of worship of God on only one day of the year? Is there not an Easter of the Church every Sunday? Surely the sacrifice on that day is not one thing and the sacrifice on this day another? Surely the splendor of the mysteries at Easter is not different from that on Sunday, Wednesday, and Friday? Whenever you commemorate Christ’s sufferings, you celebrate Easter. Formerly, lambs were sacrificed once a year, but Christ’s sacrifice is offered continually. Therefore the giver of life, making it clear that the mystery is not subject to times and days, or months and years, says to the disciples: ‘Whenever you eat this bread and drink this cup, proclaim my death.’ Who, then, celebrates that feast? Whoever performs this same mystery celebrates Easter continually.

And if they say that the mystery is performed continually, what need is there for a new feast? There is great need. Many times such a thing was given [?] to comfort our human nature and weakness. God’s mystery always remains unchanging and firm, as do the altar, the priests, the sacrifices, the acts of worship, and everything performed in his name. But because God saw human weakness, entangled with earthly matters and defiled by various kinds of impurity, he established a remedy for it through the holy apostles: the feast of Easter. Thus, whoever is always clothed in sins and fastened to earthly cares, and is unwilling to look toward the light of worship of God, might at least take notice through the name of the feast and, by remembering the life-giving sufferings, prepare himself to partake of the holy things.

Feasts exist so that many people may gather in one place, but for the saints there are feasts every day. What is the saints’ feast? To bless God. Therefore, whoever blesses him continually celebrates [?] feasts. And listen to David, who says, “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise will always be in my mouth.” Whoever blesses [?] always celebrates a feast. The names of Easter, of [?], and of feasts at which everyone assembles indicate the gathering of many in one place: to enlighten those in darkness, to bring back those who have gone astray, to straighten crooked paths, to raise the dead and buried, and, in every way, to build up all the members of Christ. But it is no wonder that those who have broken away from the Church should also separate themselves from the feast. For if they had been of us, they would have remained with us. But the corrupter of the feast will be exposed by the faithful, and our feast will shine brightly at its proper time—not as though grace were subject to particular times, for every order and arrangement is to be established in the Church. Let us now proceed with the discourse. Let us speak and preach, not regarding the preaching as something belonging to ourselves, but rendering service to the holy father. Let us discharge the overdue debt of our father’s discourse. I say this so that no one, being unaware of these circumstances, should blame us for appropriating the times allotted to our father’s teaching. For we do what we are commanded and necessarily follow our father’s wishes.

Yesterday, brothers, our task was to proclaim and discuss a little of the teaching about God at the beginning of the Gospel, and to show what intention the words reveal. John says, “In the beginning was the Word.” He did not say, “In the beginning was the Son,” or “the Only-begotten.” He strengthened the minds of his hearers, lest, through their inability to understand the teaching about God, human notions should distort the divine begetting. For among us, whenever birth is discussed, thoughts of a father and mother arise, along with bodily substance and the causes of passions. He therefore conceals the name “Son” at first and introduces the designation “Word,” so that through the designation “Word” he may explain that both the one who begets and the begetting are free from passion. And, to repeat it once again, he calls him “Word” to show that the begetting is not accompanied by passions.

“And he was with God,” he says, to make clear that his honor is undivided. He said that he was with God and showed that he is God. Then he also introduces the creation: “Everything came into being through him.” Thus the futile efforts of those who dispute will be exposed—those who seek to establish that the Only-begotten is inferior in honor because of the expressions “through him” and “by him.”

But perhaps someone will say: “Write that the heretics asked and cannot say what ‘through him’ means and what ‘by him’ means. You, who belong to the Church, explain what ‘through him’ means and what ‘by him’ means.” The divine writings do not employ the terminology of specialists or submit to constructions of human thought. For they are not Aristotelian teachings or Platonic distinctions, but sincere faith, without deceit or cunning, and full of great freedom. When Scripture says ‘through him’ and ‘by him,’ it means ‘from him’: everything is through him. What does ‘through him’ mean? Precisely this: ‘from him.’ When it says, ‘Let the waters bring forth,’ and ‘Let the earth produce,’ does it call the water and the earth creators? Or when Paul says, ‘The first man was from the earth, made of dust,’ is the earth the creator? And when he says, ‘Man did not come from woman, but woman from man,’ is the man then the woman’s [?]? Do you see that [?] ‘from him’ does not always refer to the creator, but also to some material that is involved? And it is clear that saying ‘by him’ and ‘through him’ of the giver of life does not represent him as some material put to use. Rather, he established what did not exist in existence and called what was not into being. God’s will is not like the material and timber used by craftsmen, nor is God’s essence. For his works do not proceed from God’s essence; rather, his will establishes what is not in being and what does not exist in existence. He wills, and everything comes into being; he gives a sign, and everything obeys.

And so, when it says ‘from him,’ this stands for ‘from the Father’s will’; and when it says ‘through him’ and ‘by him,’ this means precisely ‘from the Son’s power.’ And to remove this excuse from those who make excuses for sins, the blessed Paul says: ‘Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor? Or who has lent him anything and will receive repayment? For everything is from him and through him.’ If ‘through him’ indicates some inferiority, and ‘from him’ superiority in honor, how is it that here he says both of the same person? Does he mix things that cannot be mixed? And superiority in honor, ‘from him’—how is it that here he says both of the same person? Does he mix things that cannot be mixed? Of whom do they consider ‘everything is from him and through him’ to have been said: of the Father or of the Son? If of the Father, behold, they have brought the Father too down to ‘by him’ and ‘through him.’ If they have interpreted ‘by him’ and ‘through him’ as service, it would be a great insult to say ‘from him,’ ‘by him,’ and ‘through him’ of the Father, for one person cannot be both lord and servant. But was it said of the Son? Behold, there is not only ‘through him’ and ‘by him,’ but also ‘from him’; and one person cannot be both a servant and an independent agent. Rather, to clear away our delusions, he brought both expressions together in one person, so that you might learn that words do not divide God’s nature. Rather, ‘from him,’ ‘by him,’ ‘through him,’ and ‘to him’ were said of the same person, sometimes of the Father and sometimes of the Son.

And because they often repeat “by whom” and “through him,” and on that basis consider the Son to be a servant, lowly and inferior, we must gather the prophetic words and set them before you. While the blessed Joseph was in prison—he who overcame every evil through humility—he saw there the eunuchs of Pharaoh the king with sorrowful faces. Their faces revealed the grief of their hearts. “Why do you look sorrowful today?” he said. “We have had a dream,” they said, “and there is no one to interpret it for us.” And what did the blessed Joseph say to this? “Tell me the dream,” he said. He did not say that its interpretation was “from God,” but “through God.” If that is so, are you exalted while God becomes a servant? Is not the interpretation “through him,” when he ought to have said “from God”? Do you speak through God and by God, or does God speak through you and by you? So do not be enslaved to the weakness of the wording; listen to God's gifts and to the old covenants. “These are the ordinances and commandments that Moses, the servant of the Lord, commanded at the Lord's command”—that is, the commands were through Moses. Pay attention: “These,” he says, “are the ordinances and commandments that Moses commanded.” He did not say “God through Moses,” but “Moses through God.”

He said “Word,” called him God, and named him Creator; and little by little he proceeds gently to the designation “only-begotten Son.” “Everything,” he says, “came into being through him.” He proclaims his work of creation. “And without him nothing came into being”—nothing among the things that came into being, not among the uncreated nature. Do you remember the first words we spoke, that Scripture speaks with reference to the matters under discussion? For the disciples of the heretics who wage war against the Holy Spirit take “Everything came into being through him” as grounds for blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. “Everything came into being through him”—everything that came into being, and [?] the uncreated nature. When the giver of life says, “All who came before me were thieves and robbers,” will you accuse Moses of being a thief and Isaiah of being a robber? Does he not call thieves and robbers those to whom his words referred?

“Everything came into being through him, and without him nothing that came into being came into being. In him was life.” He said that he is the Word, called him God, said that he was with God, and named him Creator. He also calls him Life, because the one who is Creator is surely also the giver of life. He cannot be Creator without giving his creatures the power to live. He was Life because he possesses the gifts that give life and illumination. For whatever I established needs life and the light of life, and it cannot enjoy light without life. For this reason he immediately adds, “In him was life, and the life was the light of human beings.”

He showed the creative power, which gives life and light. Then he says, “There came to be a man sent from God, whose name was John.” Where the discourse concerns God, there is “he was”; where it concerns the man, there is “he came to be.” “He came as a witness, to testify concerning the light, so that everyone might be established through him.” The heretic finds [?] here. “Do you see,” he says, “that ‘through him’ indicates a subordinate ministry? For God himself is believed through the prophets.” But consider: although human nature stands subject to laws and to service of the Lord, here “through whom” does not indicate any subordinate ministry, but the inspiration and proclamation of the prophets. For he became a witness to the light willingly, not unwillingly. But if they persist excessively in contention and arrogance, and regard “through whom” and “through him” as signs of a subordinate ministry, let them hear Paul, who says, “God is faithful, through whom you were called into fellowship with his Son.” Here, moreover, “through whom” and “through him” do not lead from the Son to the Father, but from the Father to the Son.

“He was here in the world,” he says, “and he came into the world.” And because he said that he came into the world, lest anyone suppose that the incorporeal one underwent a change of place, he says, “He was in this world, and he came into the world.” How, they ask, can he say, “The one whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world”? Being sent does not indicate any change of place, but the manifestation of the divine dispensation. Listen to how this is so. From where does grain appear? From where does wine come? From where does oil come? Is it not from the earth? Why, then, did God say, “Behold, I am sending you grain, wine, and oil”? If the grain that is sent does not come from heaven, but its being sent is shown by the appearance of the plant, do you suppose that the incorporeal Creator, the One who is from the One who truly is, and who has being from the One who truly has being, was sent by a change of place, and not by the manifestation of the divine dispensation? For if the Son was sent from place to place, then the Father remained only there above, and the Son came only here below: the Son was not in heaven, nor [?] on earth. Pay close attention. If you are a slave to the wording and understand the Son’s being sent as though he were separated from the one who sent him, it necessarily follows that the one sent from heaven is only on earth and is separated from heaven, while the sender is not on earth but is confined to heaven. And who could be so impious and lawless, and sharpen a tongue that fights against God, as to confine the Father to heaven alone and enclose the Son only on earth?

Do you wish to learn true teaching about God, not spoken idly, but attested by the Scriptures: that the Son was sent and remained on high, and that he ascended into heaven and is with us? These are not words of my own, but those of the life-giver himself. “The one,” he says, “whom the Father sanctified and sent.” It thus seems as though he was separated from the sender. Yet how does the one who was sent say, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me,” and again, “The Father who sent me is with me”? If he is with you, then you were not sent alone, but were sent together with him. If you understand him to have been sent in a bodily manner, how can he say of the sender, the Father, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me,” and again, “The one who sent me is with me”? Lest anyone, on hearing “The one who sent me is with me,” suppose that this means some active power rather than the Father himself, he makes the statement clear elsewhere. “The Father,” he says, “who dwells in me does the works.” It is “the one who dwells in me,” not “the one who produces effects in me.”

He came from heaven and remained there in heaven. He ascended from the earth and did not depart from the earth. And since this saying is not mine, listen to the Lord himself: “I ascend,” he says, “to the Father, and I will send you the Holy Spirit.” Ascending indicates separation, and sending indicates no separation. So that no one should consider his bodily ascent a change in his divinity, he commands the disciples: “Go, make disciples of all nations, baptize them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. And behold, I am with you every day until the end of the world.” What does “I am with you” mean? From the utterance itself we recognize the Word, who spoke through the prophets then and now performs mighty deeds. “Go and make disciples of all nations, and behold, I am with you.” Who was it who said this? Clearly, it was the one who spoke through the prophet Haggai: “Now be strong, Zerubbabel, says the Lord, and let the hands of my people be strong. Work in my house, for I am with you, and my Spirit remains among you.”

God is everywhere and with all believers. The Father is among believers, the Son is among believers, and the Holy Spirit is among believers. And if you ask how the Father is among believers, listen to the prophet who says: “Rejoice and exult, daughter of Zion; exult and be glad with all your heart, for the Lord has removed the wrongs done to you and has delivered you from the hands of your enemies. He will reign in your midst; the Lord will reign in your midst, and you will no longer see evils.” Behold, the Father has been shown reigning among believers. And what of the Son? “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I too am among them.” The Father is among them, the Son is among them, and the Holy Spirit is among them: “For I am with you, says the Lord Almighty, and the Spirit remains among you.” Why do you divide those who are indivisible? [?] you break apart those who cannot be broken apart. For I am speaking of the body that he united with himself, and no one dares to say that it is separate. I know that I have spoken about this before in this same discourse, but we must not look back at what came before and leave out the teaching appropriate to the occasion. For the purpose of discourses is not to avoid going over the same things, but to keep from departing from them.

The disciples of the heretics say, “See how the Son shares equal honor with us: ‘I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’ See how the Son calls the Father his God.” Now, before everything else, we must recognize that the only-begotten Word [?], the impassible being, the incorruptible and unchangeable power, took what he had created and united flesh to himself—not descending himself into a lower condition, but raising its lower condition to a higher one. And see how he makes heavenly exchanges with humanity. For whoever makes an exchange gives and receives: he took flesh from us and gave us his Spirit. Just as you, who have a God and Lord, would not have dared to call God your Father unless you had received the Spirit from him, so the Son would not have called the Father his God unless he had taken flesh from you. For the giver of life knew that the Father was not his Father and our Father in the same way, nor his God and our God in the same manner, and so he distinguishes the names: ‘To my Father and your Father,’ because he is mine in one way and yours in another; and ‘to my God and your God,’ because he is your God in one way and mine in another. Because of the flesh taken from you, my Father became my God; and because of the Spirit received from me, God became the Father of the world. Nor could I, the Son, call the Father God if I had not taken flesh, nor would it have been possible for you to call God Father if you had not received the Spirit. Paul also bears witness: ‘Because you are sons,’ he says, ‘God sent the Spirit of his Son, who cries in your hearts, “Abba, Father.”’ I ascend to my Father by nature and to your Father by grace; to your God by nature and to my God according to my flesh.

John says, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father.” “Why,” they say, “did he not mention the Spirit? [?] the Son of God was revealed, and he said nothing about the Spirit?” We must understand, brothers, that mystical teachings are one thing and public proclamation another. In their preaching the apostles proclaimed religious teachings, but they handed down the truth in the mysteries, for it was not possible to trust dull ears and openly present an unveiled account of the Trinity. Pay attention to what Christ says to the apostles: “I still have many things to tell you, which you cannot bear now.” The apostles, who had been born among the Jews as worshipers of God, in a faith that worshiped God, who traveled with Christ, saw the signs with their own eyes, and beheld God the Word in the flesh, could not bear to hear everything at once. But how could those from among the Gentiles, who had only just escaped from pagan temples, blood, idols, and many gods—and some had not yet escaped—immediately make known the teaching of the dispensation?

The opponent of the Spirit says: “Everywhere in the Scriptures I find the Father and the Son mentioned, but silence about the Spirit. First, the Life-giver himself says, ‘No one knows the Father except the Son, and no one knows the Son except the Father.’ Did he perhaps say, ‘The Holy Spirit’? ‘No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son.’ He did not add the Spirit alongside the Father and the Son. How, then, can he be counted as belonging to the same Godhead, when he is not [?] capable of knowing the Father?”

If the Son’s knowing the Father here has sharpened your tongue to blaspheme the Spirit, what will you do if elsewhere you see it said that the Spirit knows the Father, while the Son is not mentioned? “No one has ascended into heaven,” and “No one knows the Father except the Son”: this is the voice of the Life-giver. And the same voice speaks in Paul, for he himself says, “If you wish to obtain some proof of Christ, who speaks to you through me.” And what does the voice of Christ say through Paul? “No one knows the things of a person except that person’s spirit. Likewise, no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God.” If you exclude the Spirit there, then here you must also set the Son apart. But if the Son is not excluded here, neither is the Spirit separated there.

There is also another way to consider this. Sometimes he mentions only the Father and is silent about the Son and the Spirit. Sometimes he mentions only the Son and is silent about the Father and the Spirit. Sometimes he mentions only the Spirit and is silent about the Father and the Son. Again, he very often mentions two together: he mentions the Father and the Son and is silent about the Spirit; he mentions the Son and the Spirit and is silent about the Father. Where he mentions the Father, will he be silent about the Son?

The apostles once asked Christ, “Lord, teach us to pray.” He taught them the prayer and said, “Pray in this way: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name,” and the rest, one phrase after another, to the end of the prayer. He makes no mention there of himself or of the Spirit. See: only the Father is mentioned, while the glory of the Son and of the Spirit is passed over in silence. He denies nothing, but for our benefit and for some mystical purpose, he remains silent for a time about the Spirit and the Son. “Our Father, who are in heaven”: here only the Father is mentioned. Elsewhere, see what the Life-giver himself says—the one who taught his disciples to address their prayers to the Father alone: “Whatever you ask of me, I will do for you.” He makes no mention of the Father, not to deny the Father in any way, but to speak of his own equally honored majesty. Elsewhere he mentions only the Spirit and is silent about the Father and the Son: “John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.” With the Holy Spirit alone? Then what does the explicit instruction concerning the mystery mean when it says, “Baptize them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit”? Again, he speaks of the Father and the Son and is silent about the Spirit. “There is one God, the Father,” he says, “from whom are all things, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things.” For Paul was not then discussing matters of religion, but removing the many gods from consideration. Study, and you will find the answer, just as the Life-giver says, “Search the Scriptures,” not thoughts. Do not put your trust in wandering thoughts, but listen to Scripture: “The thoughts of mortals,” it says, “are timid, and their minds are wavering.” Again the Savior says, “That they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom you sent,” and he is silent about the Spirit. Elsewhere he speaks of the Father and the Spirit and is silent about the Son, according to the testimony quoted above: “Go in and work in my house,” says the Lord Almighty, “for I am with you, and my Spirit remains among you.” And where is the Son? For he says, “I and my Spirit.” Elsewhere Paul mentions the Son and the Spirit and is silent about the Father. “Neither adulterers,” he says, “nor the sexually immoral, nor thieves, nor drunkards, nor slanderers will inherit the kingdom of God. And some of you were such people. But you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God.” And where is the Father? “Search the Scriptures,” he says, “and do not search thoughts.”

Let us also state some plain facts that reveal the lawlessness of the heretics. The apostle says, “The natural man does not accept the things of the Spirit, because they seem foolish to him.” The pagan does not stumble, because he considers the proclamation foolishness; the Jew stumbles over Christ. And what does Paul say about this? “We,” he says, “proclaim Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to pagans.” Why does the pagan consider the proclamation foolishness? Tell him that God made Christ like one of the creatures, and he does not dispute it, but says, “The Creator was able to do that.” Tell him that he was begotten, and he mocks it and considers the statement foolishness. “Can God be begotten,” he says, “whose nature is without needs?” Notice with whom the heretics have their share. The pagans disparage the teaching about his begetting as foolishness; and you make distinctions and alter the begetting, introducing a creature in place of one begotten. You are found stumbling with the Jews and considering the proclamation foolishness with the pagans. We, brothers, are not heretics. We do not find the mystery unbearable, but are enlightened by faith.

You see God proclaimed in the persons of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Before the mystery came, the prophets glorified the mystery; and do you alter the mystery proclaimed in prophecy? God spoke through the prophets as one of the persons, and at the same time imparted knowledge of the Son and the Spirit. To show the certainty of these things, and that the apostles did not proclaim this only afterward, God says something like this through the prophet Joel: “It shall be in the last days, says God.” Pay attention, for steadfast souls and attentive minds are needed here, so as not to forget the divine proclamation. “And it shall be in the last days, says God, that I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh.” For now he spoke only of himself and the Spirit, but he will also explain what concerns the Son. And what will he do? Since this is not a time for proclamation or openly professed religion, but for hidden mysteries, he introduces some intervening figures, joined together as in a parable, with many words in between, and at the end imparts knowledge of the Son. Lest making this knowledge explicit introduce occasions for sin among those unable to understand the circumstances of these things, he mentions himself and the Spirit together: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams.” And see how, while still speaking of himself and the Spirit, he gently imparts knowledge of the Son as well: “And I will give signs in heaven above and on the earth below: blood and fire and a whirlwind of smoke. The sun shall be turned to darkness and the moon to blood, before the great and manifest day of the Lord comes.” Will that day not be yours, but another Lord’s? For you announce it as though it belonged to another Lord. If you who speak are God, and you will pour out your own Spirit, how do you announce another Lord? It is indeed clear that he calls the Son who is from himself ‘Lord’: “Before the day of the Lord comes, which is great and manifest.” For the first coming took place in gentleness and quietness. He is not speaking of that coming, but of the great and manifest one, whose glory itself is evident.

And what follows this? “And it shall be,” he says, “that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.” He did not say, “Whoever calls upon my name shall be saved.” And lest the victory of the truth be thought contrived, I will bring Paul forward as a witness. What name shall we call upon and be saved? Paul, the tongue of truth and interpreter of the sayings of the prophets, says: “Is God the God of the Jews alone, and not of the Gentiles also? Yes, of the Gentiles also, since God is one, who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through that same faith.” And elsewhere: “God himself exalts all who call upon him,” and, “It shall be that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.”

And to make it clear that he applies the saying to Christ, the prophecy says, “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved,” and the apostle explains: “How shall they call upon him in whom they have not believed? And how shall they believe in him in whom they have not believed? And how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without someone preaching? And how shall they preach unless they are sent? As it is also written: ‘Beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim the good news of peace, who proclaim the good news of good things.’” He revealed himself; he also revealed the Holy Spirit, and he also revealed the Son. And just as at the beginning of the prophecy he foretold things concerning himself and the Spirit, so also at its conclusion he seals the meaning of the prophecy with the Son. For he says, “From Mount Zion shall come the one who has been saved, and those who have received the good news, whom the Lord called to himself.” By “those who have received the good news,” he means the proclaimers of the good news, who were called by the Lord. “Jesus,” he says, “called the twelve apostles and gave them authority over demons and unclean spirits.” And elsewhere, to show the royal and divine majesty of the Holy Spirit, the Spirit says concerning Paul and Barnabas: “Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for a work to which I shall call them.” And let this suffice up to this point.

May believers be enlightened, and opponents be humbled and turn back. There is no need for toil: humble yourself before the word and receive salvation. God once threatened the people of Jerusalem through the prophet, saying, “Behold, I shall destroy them and reduce them to nothing.” And when the Lord saw that their hearts had repented, the Lord said to the man of God, “Do you see how they have humbled themselves? I too shall not destroy them.” Through the prayers of the holy fathers, may they turn back, may we be strengthened, and may the Church be glorified in Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.
